Storage backend allocates request/event state; sync wrappers around asynchronous submission wait indefinitely for completion. Media cancellation changes eligible request state atomically and may decrement active count; it does not by itself cancel every physical backend operation. Driver destruction calls poweroff/unmount cleanup then destroys locks/caches/buffers/configuration records. VD/block-cache/provider bodies remain transitive obligations.

TaskCancel returns VERR_NOT_IMPLEMENTED in this tag. Endpoint close invokes its class callback then drops template reference, unlinks and frees endpoint metadata; class termination follows its endpoint lifecycle. This makes class-specific completion/drain semantics mandatory. A generic void close or canceled logical request is not a whole physical completion witness.

New tasks are atomically prepended and managers awakened. Add/close/shutdown blocking events wait indefinitely for manager acknowledgement. Endpoint close waits for tasks then releases cached tasks/ranges/file; manager destroy performs shutdown before removing events/context/heap. Allocation, queued work, worker acknowledgement and final frees are one lifetime chain; there is no independent whole-operation deadline in this handshake.

Normal manager can grow its active-request context, attempts an unlimited request count, and allocates a replacement request-handle array before freeing the old one. It waits for active AIO completion indefinitely while processing blocking events and endpoints. Request cache, new tasks, alignment buffers, locked ranges and replacement overlap need complete backing reservations; context count/bandwidth state is not a global byte/node cap.

Failsafe mode processes task lists using synchronous file flush/read/write and file growth, retaining pending tasks when rate policy prevents progress. Close/shutdown are worker states and signal a blocking-event waiter. Failsafe is not a hard-cancel or finite-storage guarantee: synchronous backend latency, write growth, rate delays, callbacks and provider final release remain part of the same domain.

POSIX cancellation calls aio_cancel. AIO_CANCELED wakes a context and waits indefinitely for acknowledgement before marking completed; ALLDONE and NOTCANCELED return distinct completion/in-progress statuses. Context waiting uses aio_suspend with timed or indefinite modes and request reconciliation. Request/context destruction depends on eligible state. These branches do not guarantee immediate backend cancellation or bounded drain, especially without the selected OS/libc implementation.

Destroy moves thread toward terminating, wakes/signals it and waits60s or150ms based on earlier success; only successful thread wait proceeds to unlink and resource destruction. The state-transition loop and wake callbacks precede that wait. A finite one-thread wait is not a total cleanup deadline or successful termination; caller policy must retain failed/live debt and all other workers/resources.

Event destruction marks invalid, broadcasts and retries busy condition/mutex destruction up to30 times with1ms sleeps per loop; errors return before free. This is attempt-count structure, not scheduler/callback elapsed-time proof. Native thread wrapper invokes common thread main then pthread_exit; native destroy here clears TLS. Common thread/refcount and Genode libc behavior remain separate from a full physical thread/stack release witness.

Close delegates to OS close and propagates errors. Flush delegates to fsync, with EINVAL returning a not-supported classification. Neither wrapper contains a timeout or proves provider/device durability or reclamation. Whole storage writer/node/backing ownership requires the selected VFS/filesystem/driver and failure policies, not merely these wrapper returns.

vCPU owns a VM-connection wrapper and halt-event handle, creates the event and switches to hardware at construction. Pause posts an exit signal or marks forced flags; halt waits at least1ms and resets its event, wake signals it. Exit constructs a temporary state reference across an EMT switch then destructs that reference. No explicit derived destructor/release method here closes the halt event or proves VM-session detached/quiescent; member/base/vendor destroy paths remain to trace. This is missing closure, not a demonstrated leak.

Semaphore create/close/signal delegate to IPRT event functions. Multi wait translates milliseconds and indefinite sentinel to relative interruptible flags; relative nanoseconds are converted to milliseconds. Several nanosecond wait variants use STOP, which logs/backtraces then sleeps forever. A supported selected call graph must exclude or control those paths; timeout/resolution constants do not establish cancel/drain/destruction of all workers. No such path was run.
